science: Astronauts sleep in sleeping bags tied to the wall, so they don't float around.
In space there's no up or down, so you can sleep any way you like.
Some astronauts wear eye masks to sleep, to keep out the many sunrises.
From the station, astronauts can see auroras: ribbons of green light near the top and bottom of the world.
At night, cities on the Earth glow like tiny golden sparkles.
parent.summary: A slow, quiet bedtime on the station: pajamas, teeth, sleeping bags on the wall, a thank-you for the day, and goodnight to the Earth.

paths.moment: Sleep right side up or upside down
options: Right side up: snug as a bug.
Upside down: lots of giggles, because in space upside down is just another way up.
Our friend Button (Button's tummy light glows pink).

beats.say: The day is done on Star Station.
The lights are low and soft, like a nightlight.
Outside the window, the Earth glows quietly.
{T}, can you give the Earth a sleepy wave? Tap anywhere.
It's time to get ready for bed.
First, cozy pajamas. One sleeve. Two sleeves. A pajama leg floated up, like a balloon.
Then, teeth. Brush, brush, brush. Little circles.
First, teeth. Brush, brush, brush. Little circles.
Then, cozy pajamas. One sleeve. Two sleeves. A pajama leg floated up, like a balloon.
Button doesn't have any teeth. So Button polished its screen, until it shone.
{T}, can you help turn the lights down? Tap, and watch them dim, one by one.
There. Soft, and sleepy.
A little drink of water before bed.
In space, drinks come in pouches, with a straw. That way, the water doesn't float away in wobbly balls.
Sip, sip. Ahhh.
Then a soft crackle came from the radio. It was Mission Control, calling from the Earth.
"Goodnight, Star Station," said Mission Control. "Thank you for all your good work today."
"Goodnight, Mission Control," said {crew}. "Thank you for helping us."
This is where the crew sleeps.
In space, we sleep in sleeping bags tied to the wall, so we don't float away while we dream.
{crew} wiggled into [their sleeping bags|a sleeping bag]. Zip. Zip.
"In space, there's no up or down," said Button. "You can sleep any way you like."
Right side up. Snug as a bug.
Upside down! {t} giggled. And then everybody giggled.
"In space, upside down is just another way up," said Button.
{T}, can you give your sleeping bag a cozy pat? Tap anywhere.
Button put on a little sleep mask. "Some astronauts wear eye masks," said Button, "to keep the sunrises out."
Before they sleep, the crew of Star Station says thank you, for one thing from today.

choice.say: {A}, what are you thankful for tonight?

beats.say: "Thank you, Earth," said {a}, "for the blue oceans, and the white clouds."
"Thank you, Button," said {a}, "for being [our|my] friend."
Button's tummy light glowed a soft, happy pink.
[{t} thought, and thought. "Thank you, stars!" said {t}.|"And thank you, stars," said {a}.]
{T}, can you make the stars twinkle a thank-you? Tap anywhere.
Button was thankful, too. "Thank you," said Button softly, "for my crew."
Outside the little window, the stars were shining.
{A}, can you count the stars with me? Tap each star, slowly.
One. Two. Three. Four. Five. Five sleepy stars.
{crew} gave a big, slow yawn. Even Button gave a little beepy yawn. Beeeep.
Out the little window, far below, ribbons of green light began to dance, over the top of the world.
"An aurora," whispered Button. "Astronauts can see them from up here."
And all across the dark Earth, the cities glowed like tiny sparkles of gold and white.
Goodnight, oceans. Goodnight, clouds.
Goodnight, little city lights. Goodnight, stars.
"Goodnight, Button." "Beep," whispered Button. "Goodnight."
[Goodnight, {A}. Goodnight, {T}.|Goodnight, {A}.]
And goodnight, Earth.
Star Station sailed on through the quiet, starry dark, around and around the world, carrying its sleepy crew.
